Frustrate
frus'trāt
v.t. (to bring to nothing, to defeat, to make void; used of God defeating men, and of men attempting to void the grace of God)
Latin frustrari, to deceive or disappoint, from frustra, in vain. The Greek in Galatians 2:21 is atheteo, to set aside, to nullify, to treat as though it had no force.

Biblical Definition

The word runs in two directions in Scripture, and the difference is everything. God frustrates: “That frustrateth the tokens of the liars, and maketh diviners mad; that turneth wise men backward, and maketh their knowledge foolish” (Isaiah 44:25). Men attempt it against Him and fail — the enemies of the returning exiles “hired counsellors against them, to frustrate their purpose” (Ezra 4:5), and the house was built. “The LORD bringeth the counsel of the heathen to nought: he maketh the devices of the people of none effect” (Psalm 33:10). But there is one thing a man can genuinely set aside, and Paul names it: “I do not frustrate the grace of God: for if righteousness come by the law, then Christ is dead in vain” (Galatians 2:21). The argument is a reductio and it is merciless. If a man could be justified by keeping the commandments, the cross was an extravagance and the death of the Son of God was pointless. To add law-keeping to grace as a ground of acceptance is therefore not a small error of proportion; it is to nullify the grace and empty the death. Paul does not say the Judaizers diminish grace. He says they set it aside altogether.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines frustrate as to defeat, to disappoint, to balk, to bring to nothing.

expand to see more

FRUSTRATE, v.t. To defeat; to disappoint; to balk; to bring to nothing; as, to frustrate a plan, design or attempt.

2. To disappoint; applied to persons.

3. To make null; to nullify; to render of no effect; as, to frustrate a conveyance.

VAIN, a. Empty; worthless; having no substance, value or importance.

NULLIFY, v.t. To annul; to make void; to render invalid; to deprive of legal force or efficacy.

Key Scripture

Galatians 2:21 — "I do not frustrate the grace of God: for if righteousness come by the law, then Christ is dead in vain."

Isaiah 44:25 — "That frustrateth the tokens of the liars, and maketh diviners mad; that turneth wise men backward, and maketh their knowledge foolish;"

Ezra 4:5 — "And hired counsellors against them, to frustrate their purpose, all the days of Cyrus king of Persia, even until the reign of Darius king of Persia."

Psalm 33:10 — "The LORD bringeth the counsel of the heathen to nought: he maketh the devices of the people of none effect."

Modern Corruption

Galatians 2:21 is read as a caution against legalistic excess, when it is a statement that law-righteousness makes the cross pointless.

expand to see more

The verse is usually softened into advice about balance — do not become too rule-bound, keep grace and works in proportion. Paul allows no proportion. His sentence is an either-or with a fatal consequence attached: if righteousness comes by the law, Christ died for nothing. Trent anathematised precisely this doctrine and taught a justification by infused grace cooperating with works; every subsequent system that makes final acceptance depend on the believer's obedience — whatever its vocabulary — falls under the same verdict. The point is not that such teaching undervalues the cross. It is that, followed out, it makes the cross unnecessary.

The mirror error is to hear frustrate the grace of God and conclude that obedience is therefore indifferent, which the next chapters of Galatians demolish. Paul who wrote this verse also wrote that they which do the works of the flesh shall not inherit the kingdom of God. Justification is by faith alone, and the faith that justifies is never alone. The Reformed distinction holds the two together where the corruptions cannot: works are excluded absolutely from the ground of acceptance and required absolutely as the fruit of it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek atheteo (G114), to set aside or nullify — Galatians 2:21, Mark 7:9; Hebrew parar and pur, to break or bring to nought — Ezra 4:5, Psalm 33:10, Isaiah 44:25.

expand to see more

Greek atheteo (G114) — to set aside, to reject, to make void; Galatians 2:21, and Mark 7:9 of rejecting the commandment of God.

Greek dorean (G1432) — in vain, without cause; Galatians 2:21, the same word rendered freely in Romans 3:24.

Hebrew parar — to break, frustrate, make void; Ezra 4:5, and used of breaking covenant.

Hebrew pur — to bring to nothing; Psalm 33:10, of the counsel of the heathen.

Isaiah 44:25 sets the pattern: God frustrates the diviner, and no man frustrates God.

Usage

"“I do not frustrate the grace of God” — the alternative is that Christ died in vain."

"“The LORD bringeth the counsel of the heathen to nought” — men are frustrated; God is not."

"To add law to grace as a ground of acceptance is to void both."
